title: Effectiveness of introducing point of care capillary testing and linking screening with routine appointments for increasing blood lead screening rates of young children: a before-after study.
ehr_evidence: Numerator data for all analyses were obtained from routinely collected data extracted from the Lead Management Program ACCESS database, which contains information on all blood lead tests conducted at both the mainstream and Indigenous health clinics.
summary: A before-after study evaluating the impact of introducing point-of-care capillary blood lead screening and linking screening with routine immunization appointments on screening participation among children aged 7-59 months resident in Broken Hill, NSW, Australia.
key_findings: Overall annual screening participation of 12-59 month old children increased from 0.39 in 2008 to 0.75 in 2012 (increase of 0.31, 95% CI increase of 0.27-0.35).

The proportion of children screened at least once by 24 months increased from 0.63 for children born in 2007 to 0.98 for children born in 2010 (0.34 increase in screening, 95% CI increase of 0.28-0.41).
The number of screening days more than doubled after screening was offered at immunization, from 80 screening days in 2010 to 184 screening days in 2012.

There was no evidence that changing to capillary sampling affected the estimate of the underlying population blood lead level; geometric means fluctuated at or slightly below previously observed levels.
pathologies_diseases: Blood lead exposure / elevated blood lead levels (lead poisoning risk)
study_design: Before-after study (quasi-experimental, single-community, no control group)
population: Children aged 7-59 months (1-4 years old) resident in Broken Hill, NSW, Australia
limitations: Before-after study design limited the ability to examine other factors that might have influenced screening rates and to rule out that offering venous screening at routine visits may have similarly increased attendance.
No control community, so broader factors (e.g., national health promotion campaigns) could not be ruled out.

Denominators were estimated from census data and the NSW Midwives Database, introducing uncertainty due to assumed linear change between censuses, time delays in data entry, and lack of in/out migration accounting.
